<explanation>
Based on your project’s file structure and README, Pensieve (formerly known as Memos) is a full‐stack application focused on passive screen recording, image indexing (using OCR, vector embeddings, and visual search via VLM), and a convenient web interface for retrieval. Its architecture is split across several distinct areas: screen capture, event-based processing, plugin-driven data extraction/indexing, data persistence (using either SQLite or PostgreSQL), and a modern Svelte-based front end.

Below are detailed guidelines and instructions to design an accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components and Layers:
   • Screenshot Recording Component:
     - Represent the “memos record” functionality (and the “screen_recorder” module) that actively captures screenshots.
   • Event Watching and Processing Component:
     - Show the “memos watch” service that listens for new screenshot events.
     - This part dynamically submits indexing jobs and delegates processing tasks.
   • Data Processing and Plugin Layer:
     - Include components for OCR and VLM plugins (located under memos/plugins/ocr and memos/plugins/vlm).
     - Identify where embedding modules and the simple tokenizer exist.
     - Include connections to the external ML backends (in memos_ml_backends) which serve specialized functionalities for ML-powered indexing.
   • API/Web Server Component:
     - Represent the “memos serve” (and memos/main.py) which runs the web server providing access and a dashboard.
     - It processes indexing/search requests.
   • Frontend Component:
     - Depict the web interface project (“web” folder). This Svelte-based UI interacts with the backend via defined API endpoints.
   • Database Storage:
     - Show a persistence layer that might use SQLite by default, with optional enhanced performance using PostgreSQL (with pgvector extension).
   • Background Services & CLI:
     - Optionally add a note that the system can be manipulated from the command line (via “memos init”, “memos start”, “memos migrate”, etc.) and that the service can run in separate processes.

2. Establish Relationships and Integration:
   • Draw directional arrows to illustrate data flow:
     - Screenshots are captured by the recording service → sent to the watch/processing module.
     - Processors apply OCR, embeddings, and VLM plugin operations to extract text and image metadata.
     - Processed results are cached/indexed and then stored in the database.
     - The API/web server reads from the database and serves data to the frontend.
     - Optionally, annotate that the CLI commands can trigger configuration, migration, or manual re-indexing of screenshots.
   • Indicate optional routes such as switching from local SQLite to a PostgreSQL backend via configuration editing.
  
3. Point Out Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Separation of Concerns: Distinguish between services for capturing, processing, indexing, and serving data.
   • Modular Extensibility: Emphasize the plugins (for OCR, VLM, etc.) demonstrating a modular design that allows adding or replacing functionality.
   • Event-Driven Processing: Use an event or watch pattern for asynchronous processing of screenshots.
   • Client-Server Architecture: Highlight the Svelte-based frontend communicating with a Python-powered backend via a REST or similar API.
   • Scalability Aspect: Note the separation of ML processing tasks and the dedicated database layer, especially when using PostgreSQL for large-scale data.

4. Include Relevant Technologies and Libraries:
   • Python Core with its CLI commands, configuration (YAML-based), and migrations using Alembic.
   • Use of Docker for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension.
   • Svelte for the front end.
   • External integrations such as Ollama for multimodal visual search.
   • Tools like alembic for database migration and logging modules for tracking operations.

5. Tailoring the Diagram for a Full-Stack Application:
   • Clearly separate backend services (recording, processing, indexing, web serving) from the frontend presentation layer.
   • Show how the web interface interacts through API endpoints with the backend.
   • If relevant, depict the configurable nature of the database (SQLite vs. PostgreSQL) by using different icons or noting configuration file switches.

6. Visual Notations for the Diagram:
   • Use clear, labeled boxes representing each component or module.
   • Add directional arrows to indicate data flows:
       – For example, an arrow from “Screenshot Capture (memos record)” → “Event Watcher (memos watch)” → “Processing Plugins (OCR/VLM/Embedding)” → “Database”.
       – Parallel arrows for control flow going to and from the “CLI Commands” component.
   • Apply color coding or distinct shapes to differentiate layers:
       – Use one color or shape for system services (record, watch, serve), a different style for plugins/extensions, and another for external services (database, Docker-based PostgreSQL, external ML endpoints).
   • Clearly label external interfaces (e.g., REST API, Docker Container for PostgreSQL, Web UI).

7. Ending with Detailed, Component-Based Instructions:
   • Remind the engineer to include every key piece: the screenshot recording process, event-based indexing, plugin integration for OCR/VLM and embedding, the data persistence layer, and the web service with its user interface.
   • Emphasize that even if there are several sub-components (e.g., migrations, configuration, logging), each should be represented to capture the full picture of how data flows through the system.
   • Encourage using a diagram tool that supports layering if possible – for example, diagramming platforms like Lucidchart, draw.io, or Visio that will allow clear arrows, color coding, and annotations.

This design will result in a diagram that visually decomposes Pensieve into its main parts:
   - The screenshot capture and recording system.
   - The event-driven processor handling indexing (with both OCR and ML-based visual search modules).
   - The flexible, RESTful web server delivering content to a Svelte-based frontend.
   - The underlying configurable database that can swap from SQLite to PostgreSQL.
   - The integration with external ML backends for enhanced image understanding.

Using these detailed guidelines, the principal software engineer can create a comprehensive and accurate system design diagram that covers the “big picture” along with the essential technical details relevant to Pensieve’s architecture.
</explanation>
